However, to convey complex meanings and relationships, Swahili speakers rely on a range of syntactical mechanisms, including relative clauses, subordinate clauses, and discourse markers.

Relative clauses in Swahili are formed using the prefix "ye-" or "yo-", which agrees with the noun class of the head noun. For example, "mwanafunzi ye anaye soma" (the student who is reading) uses the prefix "ye-" to agree with the noun class "m-/wa-" (human beings). Subordinate clauses, on the other hand, are introduced by subordinating conjunctions such as "kwa kuwa" (because) or "kama" (if). These clauses can be used to express cause-and-effect relationships, conditions, or contrasts.

Discourse markers play a crucial role in connecting ideas and organizing text in Swahili. Markers such as "kwa hiyo" (therefore) and "kwa kuwa" (because) help to signal the relationships between clauses and sentences, while others, like "lakini" (but) and "hata" (even), indicate contrast or addition. By using these markers effectively, speakers can construct coherent and persuasive texts, including narratives, arguments, and explanations.

For example, the use of honorifics and polite language can affect the tone and style of a text, while the speaker's intention and audience can influence the choice of vocabulary and syntax.
